title: The funeral
hook: eulogy, psalms, and the prayer "God full of mercy"

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was keriah, and your line was the tear: grief made visible. Today the mourners, torn garments and all, walk into the funeral.

No flowers on the plain wooden coffin. Folding chairs, a small chapel, people in coats they don't wear often. A grandson unfolds a sheet of paper and tells a story about fishing that makes the whole room laugh, then go quiet. Someone reads a psalm. Then the cantor, or a rabbi, or a friend who knows the tune, begins to sing in Hebrew, slow, rising and falling, and in the middle of it comes a name: the name of the person in the coffin, sung out loud. Today's word is that song.
screen: `A PLAIN COFFIN, NO FLOWERS.` → `A STORY ABOUT FISHING.` → `A NAME, SUNG OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: It's El Male Rachamim, God full of mercy. But first the eulogy, the hesped, which you met in your first year with Abraham. When Sarah dies, Genesis says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her." The rabbis saw a eulogy there. A hesped is meant to do both: speak about the person, and let people weep. The codes ask the speaker to praise truly, not to invent a saint, because an honest picture honors the dead more than a flattering one. Psalms are read, and Psalm twenty-three may be among them: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." It's read as company for the road, not as an explanation. Then the prayer. El Male Rachamim is a short memorial prayer, usually sung. It calls on God full of mercy, who dwells on high, to give true rest to the soul of the one who has died, beneath the wings of the divine presence, and it names them. It asks that their soul be bound up in the bond of life. It may be sung again at the grave, and later on days of remembrance. In the middle of that slow melody, one ordinary name is sung as if it belongs there. The funeral says out loud, together, that this person mattered, and hands them, by name, to mercy.
screen: `THE HESPED: SPEAK TRULY.` · `THE LORD IS MY SHEPHERD.` · `REST BENEATH THE WINGS.` · `ONE NAME, SUNG.` · then, large: `GOD FULL OF MERCY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone grieving now, or who lost someone this year, and picture them in a crowded room after the service. Think what it would mean simply to sit beside them, no speech, maybe the name of the one they lost said gently, so they hear it again; if you pray, hold that name in your prayer. And if your own grief ever feels too heavy, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
El Male Rachamim. God full of mercy: the sung memorial prayer that asks rest for the soul and says the person's name. Today's word.
Your line: god full of mercy. A name said with love is never small. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: A Jewish funeral is usually simple: a eulogy (hesped), psalms, and the memorial prayer El Male Rachamim, sung by a cantor or rabbi with the name of the person who died; it is often sung again at the graveside.

chat.says: At the funeral, why did they sing a prayer with his name in it?
options: El Male Rachamim asks God full of mercy to give his soul rest, naming him.
It calls his soul back for one last goodbye before the burial.
Singing his name announces that he's already been judged and forgiven.
chat.meaning: El Male Rachamim asks God full of mercy for true rest for the soul, and names the person, handing them, by name, to mercy.

El Male Rachamim described, not quoted or translated in full: God full of mercy who dwells on high, true rest beneath the wings of the Shechinah, bound in the bond of life (1 Samuel 25:29). Confirm summary.
Shulchan Aruch YD 344 (eulogize truly; slight but not great exaggeration) paraphrased as 'praise truly, not invent a saint'; confirm.
'Psalm twenty-three is often among them' and 'sung again at the grave, and later on days of remembrance' kept general; confirm. Note: the index carry 'god full of mercy' is lowercase; kept exactly.
Genesis 23:2 read as the source of the hesped (Hebrew lispod): confirm the rabbinic reading.
No flowers at the funeral: customary in many communities; confirm.
